records.title: Ijapa the Tortoise and the Gourd of Wisdom
records.summary: A foundational trickster narrative in Yoruba oral folklore, Ijapa the tortoise schemes to monopolize all the wisdom of the earth. Gathering every proverb, craft, and understanding into a hollowed calabash gourd, he ties it around his neck and attempts to climb a tall palm tree to hide it high in the canopy where no other mortal or animal can reach it. However, with the bulky gourd tied to his front, he repeatedly slips down the trunk. His young son watching from the grass shouts: 'Father, why not tie the gourd to your back so your hands and chest can grip the bark?' Realizing his child possessed wisdom that escaped him, Ijapa hurls the calabash to the ground in frustration, shattering it so wisdom scattered across the four corners of the world for everyone to share.
alternate_names: The Tortoise and the Gourd of Knowledge

records.title: The Heroism of Queen Moremi Ajasoro
records.summary: In ancient Ile-Ife, the spiritual cradle of the Yoruba people, the kingdom was repeatedly terrorized by bizarre raiders known as the Igbo (forest masqueraders), who appeared as terrifying, invulnerable apparitions covered in raffia and bush vegetation. Distressed by her people's suffering, Queen Moremi Ajasoro made a solemn vow to the river spirit Esimirin: if the goddess granted her the secret to defeat the raiders, Moremi would sacrifice whatever first came to meet her upon her return. Allowing herself to be captured, Moremi used her beauty and intelligence to marry the enemy king and discover their weakness: the raffia suits were flammable. Escaping to Ile-Ife, she instructed her warriors to attack with firebrands, routing the raiders. Returning home, she discovered her only son Oluorogbo ran to greet her, fulfilling her tragic sacrifice.
community_attributions: Ooni of Ife royal palace historians

records.title: Sango the Thunder King of the Oyo Empire
records.summary: Sango (Shango) was the historically formidable third Alaafin (Emperor) of the ancient Oyo Empire, renowned for his fiery temper, military brilliance, and mastery over lightning. Wielding a double-headed bronze axe (oshe) and riding into battle breathing smoke and sparks, Sango could summon thunderbolts from the heavens to incinerate enemy armies. Following a bitter political dispute between his two top generals, Timi and Gbonka, which led to civil strife and the burning of his capital, Sango retreated into the forest and hanged himself from an ayan tree in remorse. Loyal devotees proclaimed 'Oba kò so' ('The King did not hang!'), witnessing him ascend directly into the heavens to become the Orisha of thunder, lightning, and cosmic justice.
alternate_names: Oba Kò So (The King Did Not Hang)
records.historical_period: c. 14th–15th Century Old Oyo Empire (deified post-reign)

records.title: Oya the Fierce Goddess of the River Niger
records.summary: Oya is the fierce Yoruba Orisha of winds, hurricanes, lightning, and rebirth, venerated as the patron deity of the great River Niger (known traditionally as Odò Oya). As the warrior-queen and consort of Sango, she rides alongside him into the storm wielding a machete of bronze and waving a fly-whisk (irukere) that summons tornadoes. According to sacred folklore, Oya also commands the transition between life and death as the guardian of the cemetery gates and master of the ancestral masquerades (Egungun), capable of shapeshifting into a fierce water buffalo to defend her devotees from injustice.
alternate_names: The Lady of the River Niger
records.region_or_community: Niger River basin, Kwara and Oyo States

records.title: Queen Amina of Zazzau: The Warrior Queen
records.summary: Ruling the Hausa kingdom of Zazzau (modern-day Zaria in northern Nigeria) during the late 16th century, Queen Amina was a legendary military commander who expanded her empire across the savanna from Kano to the Niger River. Refusing to marry permanently, Amina led a formidable cavalry force into battle personally, clad in iron chainmail and wielding a lance. She pioneered the construction of colossal defensive mud-brick fortifications surrounding every conquered city, known throughout northern Nigeria as Ganuwar Amina (Amina's Walls). Hausa oral epics celebrate her as 'Amina, woman as capable as a man' (Amina yar Bakwa ta san rana).
records.historical_period: Late 16th Century (reign c. 1576–1610, chronicled in Kano Chronicle)
records.region_or_community: Zazzau (Zaria), Kaduna and Kano States, Northern Nigeria

records.title: The Sacred Waters of Osun-Osogbo
records.summary: In the lush forested river bend of Osogbo, the sacred river goddess Osun is venerated as the compassionate Orisha of fertility, sweet waters, maternal love, and gold. When founding chieftain Larooye arrived at the Osun River during a severe drought, a gentle voice rose from the rushing waters promising that if the people honored her sanctuary and preserved the pristine canopy of the river grove, the settlement would flourish and childless women would conceive. The sacred agreement established the enduring Osun-Osogbo festival, where the virgin maiden Arugba carries the sacred calabash of offerings to the river each August.
records.historical_period: Pre-Colonial Yoruba settlement (enshrined as UNESCO World Heritage Site)

records.title: The Hunter and the Forest Spirits of Igbale
records.summary: In traditional Yoruba hunting lore, master hunters (Ode) undergo rigorous spiritual apprenticeships to perceive the hidden dimensions of the deep virgin jungle (Igbale). A veteran hunter tracks an elusive antelope into a hidden clearing where the trees whisper and the soil is made of brass. Peering through the leaves, he witnesses the antelope shed its skin to become a beautiful maiden dancing with forest spirits (Aroni and Ijimere). Warned by the spirits never to reveal their secret dwelling or hunt without protective medicinal amulets (oogun), the hunter returns home enriched with herbal knowledge, teaching future generations the sacred taboos of forest conservation.
alternate_names: The Hunter and the Shapeshifting Antelope
records.historical_period: Traditional Yoruba Oral Poetry (preserved in Ijala hunting chants)
records.region_or_community: Ekiti, Ondo, and Osun forested hinterlands

records.title: The Origin of Death and the Slow Chameleon
records.summary: In early times when humanity lived peacefully without sickness or mortality, the Supreme Creator Olodumare decided that mortals should live forever. He entrusted this joyful message of eternal life to the deliberate, slow-moving Chameleon (Oga), commanding him to walk to the mortal realm. On the long journey, the Chameleon took careful, hesitant steps, constantly admiring the colors of leaves and testing each branch. Impatient with the delay, the swift-flying Lizard (Alangba) rushed to earth ahead of him and mischievously proclaimed: 'The Creator says: All mortals shall die and return to dust!' When the Chameleon finally arrived with the truth, humanity had already accepted the false message, cementing the permanent presence of death on earth.
records.region_or_community: Pan-Nigerian indigenous folklore (Yoruba, Igbo, and Edo traditions)
geographic_associations: Traditional ancestral lands of Southern Nigeria

records.title: The Palm-Wine Drinkard and the Town of the Deads
records.summary: A legendary milestone of 20th-century Nigerian literature based directly on Yoruba oral folklore, a young man who does nothing all day but drink palm wine embarks on a surreal quest to the 'Deads' Town' following the accidental death of his master palm-wine tapster. Journeying through uncanny spirit forests, he confronts the 'Complete Gentleman'—a handsome traveler who rented human limbs, flesh, and skin to impress a bride, returning each part to creditors until only a bouncing skull remained—and battles immense monstrous spirits using traditional magical charms (juju), capturing the surreal, terrifying logic of traditional Yoruba ghostlore.
records.historical_period: Modern Nigerian Literary Folklore (published 1952 by Amos Tutuola)
records.region_or_community: Abeokuta, Ogun State and Yoruba hinterlands

records.title: The Clever Goat and the Greedy Leopard
records.summary: In this classic Edo and Benin kingdom animal fable, an industrious he-goat decides to build a stone house in the forest. Unknown to him, a ferocious leopard selects the exact same clearing. While the goat gathers timber by day, the leopard arrives by night to erect the walls, each assuming a friendly forest deity is helping with the construction. When the house is completed, both move in simultaneously and discover each other. The trembling goat uses sharp wits: when the leopard brings home a slaughtered antelope for dinner, the goat loudly grumbles that the meat is too small and demands a leopard carcass instead. Terrified by the goat's apparent ferocity, the leopard flees the house forever.
alternate_names: The Shared House in the Forest
geographic_associations: Benin City ancient moats and forest reserves
